aftermath/0.text: Mir Jafar got the throne, exactly as promised. The Company got the treasury, also exactly as promised — and then kept collecting.

battle/0.text: The scoreboard looked absurd. Fifty thousand soldiers and fifty-three cannon for the Nawab. Three thousand men for the Company.

battle/1.text: Then, at noon, the monsoon opened. The Nawab's gunners left their powder in the rain. The Company put tarpaulins over theirs.

battle/2.text: When the Nawab's wet cannon went quiet, the Company's dry ones did not. And Mir Jafar's third of the army watched. Very still. Very neutral.

battle/3.text: By evening the Nawab's army was a rumor. Siraj left early.

bengal/0.text: In 1756, the richest province of the crumbling Mughal Empire was Bengal — silk, saltpetre, and one fifth of all the money in Asia.

bengal/1.text: Everybody wanted a piece. The French had a trading post. The British East India Company had a bigger one, with walls.

calcutta-falls/0.text: In June 1756 the Nawab marched fifty thousand men from Murshidabad and took Calcutta in four days.

calcutta-falls/1.text: The Company was not used to losing warehouses. From Madras it sent its most reliable fixer — Robert Clive — with ships.

calcutta-falls/2.text: Calcutta changed hands again in January. Nobody apologized.

conspiracy/0.text: Fighting fifty thousand men is expensive. Bribing their commander is not. The Company found Mir Jafar, the Nawab's own general, and made him an offer.

conspiracy/1.text: The terms were simple. The army stands still, Jafar becomes Nawab, and the Company gets the treasury.

epilogue/0.text: The battle took one afternoon and cost the Company twenty-two men. The receipt — an empire — took two hundred years to pay off.

nawab/0.text: Bengal's new ruler was Siraj ud-Daulah — twenty-three years old, freshly crowned, and deeply unimpressed by unauthorized walls.

plassey-morning/0.text: On the twenty-third of June, 1757, the two armies met in a mango grove by the river at Plassey.
